title: Jeppesen ForeFlight's Device-as-a-Service EFB Model Is a Bet That Airlines Want to Buy Outcomes, Not Platforms
summary: The Manage My EFB launch from Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix repackages the airline EFB program as a per-device subscription — and the commercial logic behind that shift is worth unpacking.
body_markdown:
When Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix Corporation announced their jointly developed Manage My EFB offering in June, the headline framed it as a Device-as-a-Service play — and that framing is accurate as far as it goes. But the more interesting read is what this product says about how the EFB market is maturing and where the competitive pressure is actually coming from.

## What the Model Actually Does

<cite index="16-3">Manage My EFB is available exclusively through Jeppesen ForeFlight and introduces a subscription-based delivery model that bundles devices, EFB software, Stratix lifecycle services, and connectivity into a single, predictable cost per device, per month.</cite> The device in question is the Apple iPad, with Stratix handling procurement, deployment, and ongoing lifecycle management while ForeFlight supplies the software layer. <cite index="16-5">The offering is designed to scale from regional operators to global carriers, supporting both commercial and business aviation customers.</cite>

On its face, this looks like a convenience product. In practice, it's a structural change in how ForeFlight enters and retains airline accounts. Rather than selling a software license and leaving the airline to figure out its own device procurement, MDM, connectivity contracts, and refresh cycles, the bundle absorbs all of that into a single vendor relationship. The airline's EFB administrator stops managing four or five separate vendor relationships and starts managing one line item on a monthly invoice.

## The Commercial Logic Is Stronger Than It Looks

For ForeFlight, the strategic value here isn't the hardware — Stratix handles that — it's the stickiness that comes from owning the full program rather than just the software tier. Airlines that have committed their entire EFB lifecycle to a single bundled subscription are meaningfully harder to displace than airlines that licensed software and can swap it independently of their device contract. The switching cost isn't just technical re-evaluation; it's unwinding a managed service relationship.

From Stratix's side, aviation is a demanding but attractive vertical: fleets are predictable in size, device refresh cycles are operationally driven rather than arbitrary, and compliance documentation requirements create natural demand for the kind of audit trail and lifecycle management that enterprise mobility firms already do well. <cite index="16-6,16-7">Stratix brings over 40 years of experience designing, deploying, and managing comprehensive mobility programs</cite> — and aviation's requirements, while specific, map reasonably well onto what Stratix already does for large enterprise customers in other regulated industries.

For airlines, the pitch is essentially an opex conversion: capital expenditure for devices and software becomes a predictable per-device monthly cost with no surprise refresh cycles. That's a genuine budgeting advantage for operators who've historically had to justify lump-sum EFB fleet refresh investments on a multi-year cycle.

## What This Signals About EFB Competition

The deeper signal here is that EFB competition among commercial operators is no longer purely about features. The incumbents — ForeFlight, Lido, Aviobook, Bytron's skybook — are increasingly differentiated not just by what the software does but by how easy it is to deploy, manage, and sustain at scale. A mid-size carrier that doesn't want to build internal MDM expertise for 300 pilot devices is a natural buyer for something like Manage My EFB, even if it would have preferred a different software platform on pure feature grounds.

That dynamic has real implications for smaller or newer EFB vendors trying to break into commercial aviation accounts. A bundled, fully managed subscription from an incumbent is harder to dislodge on a competitive bid than a standalone software license — and that's probably the point. Having spent years on the delivery and deployment side of aviation tech programs, I've seen how much friction lives in the gap between software selection and full fleet rollout. Any vendor that credibly closes that gap as part of the initial sale changes the competitive calculus for everyone else in the room.

Whether airlines actually want a single vendor managing the full stack — or whether they'll resist that consolidation to preserve flexibility — is the open question. But as a commercial move, it's a well-timed one.

email_brief: Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix Corporation announced Manage My EFB in June 2026 — a Device-as-a-Service offering that bundles Apple iPads, ForeFlight EFB software, Stratix lifecycle management, and connectivity into a single per-device monthly subscription, available exclusively through ForeFlight. Today's post frames this as a commercial strategy story: the bundle shifts EFB competition from pure software features toward total program management, and raises real questions about how airlines weigh switching costs when a vendor owns the full stack. It's relevant right now because EFB platform differentiation is intensifying — several posts this month have covered ForeFlight's AI feature push, Aviobook's weather data integration, and the broader question of what actually drives airline EFB platform decisions.
